For \(k=1,\ldots,n\), the \emph{tail matrix} of level \(k\) is
\[
 B_{\geq k}:=\big[\, B_k\mid B_{k+1} \mid \cdots \mid B_n \,\big].
\]
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
The sequence \((w_1,\ldots,w_n)\) is called the
\emph{tail rank profile} of \(B\).
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
A basis
\(\mathcal B=\big(b_{j_1}^1,\ldots,b_{j_d}^d\big)\) of \(V\) is called a
\emph{basis of representatives compatible with the flag}
\eqref{eq:flag} if, for every \(k=1,\ldots,n\),
\[
 \operatorname{Span}\big(\mathcal B_{\geq k}\big)=W_k,
 \qquad
 \mathcal B_{\geq k}
 :=
 \big\{b_{j_s}^s\in\mathcal B:j_s\geq k \big\}.
\]
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:required}
Let \(\mathcal B=\big(b_{j_1}^1,\ldots,b_{j_d}^d \big)\) be a basis of
representatives compatible with the flag. Then, for every
\(k=1,\ldots,n\),
\[
 \#\big\{i:j_i=k \big\}=w_k-w_{k+1}=r_k.
\]
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Since \(\mathcal B\) is a basis, every subfamily is linearly
independent. Compatibility therefore gives
\(\#\mathcal B_{\geq k}=\dim W_k=w_k\) and
\(\#\mathcal B_{\geq k+1}=w_{k+1}\).
Their difference is precisely the number of vectors selected from
the \(k\)-th block, which proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:quota-characterization}
Let \(\mathcal B=\big(b_{j_1}^1,\ldots,b_{j_d}^d\big)\) be a basis of
representatives. Then \(\mathcal B\) is compatible with the
tail-space flag if and only if
\[
 \#\big\{i:j_i=k\big\}=r_k,
 \qquad k=1,\ldots,n.
\]
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Necessity follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:required}.

Conversely, suppose that
\(\#\{i:j_i=k\}=r_k\) for every \(k\). Fix \(k\). 
Then
\[
 \#\mathcal B_{\geq k}
 =
 \sum_{j=k}^n r_j
 =
 w_k.
\]
Since \(\mathcal B_{\geq k}\) is a subfamily of the basis
\(\mathcal B\), it is linearly independent, and hence
\(\dim\operatorname{Span}\big(\mathcal B_{\geq k}\big)=w_k\).

Every vector in \(\mathcal B_{\geq k}\) belongs to one of the blocks
\(B_k,\ldots,B_n\). Hence
\[
 \operatorname{Span}\big(\mathcal B_{\geq k}\big)\subseteq W_k.
\]
Since both spaces have dimension \(w_k\), they are equal.
 Thus
\(\operatorname{Span}\big(\mathcal B_{\geq k} \big)=W_k\) for every \(k\), and
\(\mathcal B\) is compatible with the tail-space flag.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The numbers \(r_k\) are determined entirely by the matrix \(B\).
They specify how many representatives a compatible basis must select
from each block \(B_k\). Conversely, once a representative system is
known to be a basis, these block counts are sufficient for
compatibility: it is compatible with the tail-space flag if and only if
it selects exactly \(r_k\) vectors from \(B_k\) for every \(k\).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:trimming}
Let \(k_0=\max\big\{k:w_k=d\big\}\). Then
\(r_1=\cdots=r_{k_0-1}=0\). Consequently, no compatible basis of
representatives contains a vector from
\(B_1,\ldots,B_{k_0-1}\), and the compatible-basis problem for \(B\)
is equivalent to the same problem for the trimmed matrix
\[
 B_{\mathrm{trim}}:=B_{\geq k_0}.
\]
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
By definition of \(k_0\),
\(w_1=\cdots=w_{k_0}=d\), so
\(r_j=w_j-w_{j+1}=0\) for every \(j<k_0\).
By Proposition~\ref{prop:quota-characterization}, a compatible basis
therefore uses no representatives from
\(B_1,\ldots,B_{k_0-1}\). These blocks may consequently be deleted
without changing either the existence or the set of compatible bases.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
\label{problem:compatiblebasis}
Given a block matrix \(B\) of full row rank, determine whether it
admits a basis of representatives compatible with its tail-space flag,
and construct one whenever it exists.
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
A \emph{single-use actuator schedule} is a map
\[
 \tau:\{1,\ldots,d\}\longrightarrow\{1,\ldots,N\},
\]
where \(\tau(i)\) is the control slot in which actuator \(i\) is used.
Different actuators may be assigned to the same slot.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
A single-use schedule \(\tau\) is called
\emph{terminally controllable} if the selected directions span
\(\mathbb R^d\), equivalently,
\[
 \operatorname{rank}
 \big[\, A^{N-\tau(1)}g_1\ \cdots\ A^{N-\tau(d)}g_d\,\big]
 =d.
\]
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
A single-use actuator schedule \(\tau\) is called
\emph{reachability-profile preserving} if
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:profilepreserving}
 \operatorname{Span}\big\{
 A^{N-\tau(i)}g_i:\tau(i)\geq k
 \big\}
 =
 W_k
\end{equation}
for every \(k=1,\ldots,N\).
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:two-actuators}
Let \(d=2\), \(N=3\), and consider
\[
 A=
 \begin{bmatrix}
 1&0\\
 1&1
 \end{bmatrix},
 \qquad
 G=I_2=[g_1,g_2].
\]
Thus \(g_1=(1,0)^T\) and \(g_2=(0,1)^T\).

The two columns of \(G\) describe the instantaneous directions of the
two actuators. The matrix \(A\) describes how these directions evolve
between consecutive control slots. In particular,
\(Ag_1=(1,1)^T\) and \(Ag_2=(0,1)^T\).

Since \(N=3\), the three slot matrices are
\[
 B_1=A^2G=
 \begin{bmatrix}
 1&0\\
 2&1
 \end{bmatrix},
 \qquad
 B_2=AG=
 \begin{bmatrix}
 1&0\\
 1&1
 \end{bmatrix},
 \qquad
 B_3=G=
 \begin{bmatrix}
 1&0\\
 0&1
 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The columns of \(B_1\) are the terminal effects of firing the two
actuators in the first slot, those of \(B_2\) correspond to the second
slot, and those of \(B_3\) to the final slot. Thus
\[
 B=\big[\,B_1\mid B_2\mid B_3\,\big]= \big[\,A^2G\mid AG\mid G\,\big]
\]
collects all possible actuator--slot choices.

Consider the schedule
\[
 \tau(1)=1,\qquad \tau(2)=3.
\]
It selects the first column of \(B_1\) and the second column of \(B_3\),
namely \(A^2g_1=(1,2)^T\) and \(g_2=(0,1)^T\).
With amplitudes \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\),
\[
 x_3
 =
 \alpha_1(1,2)^T+\alpha_2(0,1)^T.
\]
These two directions are linearly independent, so the schedule is
terminally controllable.

It is not, however, reachability-profile preserving. At the beginning
of slot \(2\), actuator \(1\) has already been used, and only actuator
\(2\) remains available. Hence the remaining selected directions span
only \(\operatorname{Span}\{g_2\}\). On the other hand, the unrestricted system still
has both actuators available in slots \(2\) and \(3\), and
\(W_2=\mathbb R^2\). Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Span}\{g_2\}\neq W_2.
\]

By contrast, the schedule
\[
 \tau(1)=\tau(2)=3
\]
keeps both actuators available until the last slot. Their terminal
directions are then \(g_1\) and \(g_2\), and the schedule preserves
the complete reachability profile.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
A concrete physical picture is an idealized small satellite equipped
with two one-shot thrusters. The columns of \(G\) describe the
instantaneous state changes produced by the two thrusters, while
\(A\) describes how these changes propagate through the subsequent
dynamics.

Firing a thruster in an early slot may strongly influence the terminal
state because its effect is propagated for several time steps. Once
fired, however, that thruster is no longer available for later
corrections. In Example~\ref{ex:two-actuators}, firing actuator \(1\)
in the first slot still allows full terminal controllability, but it
removes one control direction from the remaining part of the horizon.
The profile-preserving condition prevents this premature loss of
future control authority.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:equivalence}
Let \(B_j=A^{N-j}G\). There is a one-to-one correspondence between
reachability-profile preserving single-use actuator schedules and
bases of representatives compatible with the tail-space flag of \(B\).
The correspondence is
\[
 \tau
 \longmapsto
 \mathcal B(\tau)
 =
 \big(b_{\tau(1)}^1,\ldots,b_{\tau(d)}^d \big).
\]
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
A schedule chooses, for each actuator \(i\), exactly one indexed vector
\(b_{\tau(i)}^i\), and hence determines a representative system.

If the schedule is profile preserving, the condition for \(k=1\)
shows that the selected \(d\) vectors span \(\mathbb R^d\), and hence
form a basis. For every \(k\), the vectors corresponding to actuators
scheduled in slots \(k,\ldots,N\) are precisely
$
 \{b_{\tau(i)}^i:\tau(i)\geq k\}.
$
Therefore condition \eqref{eq:profilepreserving} is exactly the
compatibility condition with the tail space \(W_k\). The converse is
identical.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:schedule-characterization}
A single-use actuator schedule \(\tau\) is reachability-profile
preserving if and only if
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item it is terminally controllable, that is,
\[
 \operatorname{rank}
 \big[\, A^{N-\tau(1)}g_1\ \cdots\ A^{N-\tau(d)}g_d\, \big]
 =d;
\]
\item exactly \(r_k=w_k-w_{k+1}\) actuators are assigned to slot
\(k\), that is,
\[
 \#\big\{i:\tau(i)=k \big\}=r_k,
 \qquad k=1,\ldots,N.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:equivalence}, the schedule corresponds to the
representative system \(\mathcal B(\tau)\). Condition (i) says that
this system is a basis, while condition (ii) gives the block quotas.
The result follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop:quota-characterization}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Let \(d=4\), \(n=3\), with
\[
 (r_1,r_2,r_3)=(1,1,2),
 \qquad
 (w_1,w_2,w_3)=(4,3,2),
\]
and
\[
 B_1=[0,0,e_4,0],\qquad
 B_2=[e_3,0,e_1+e_2,e_2],\qquad
 B_3=[e_1,e_2,0,0].
\]
For the partial selection
\[
 S=\{b_3^1,b_3^2\}=\{e_1,e_2\},
\]
we have \(I(S)=\{3,4\}\) and \(u_3(S)=2=r_3\). Hence, at level
\(k=2\),
\[
 R_{\geq2}(S)
 =
 \{b_2^3,b_2^4\}
 =
 \{e_1+e_2,e_2\}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \dim\operatorname{Span}\bigl(S_{\geq2}\cup R_{\geq2}(S)\bigr)
 =2<3=w_2,
\]
so the partial selection cannot be completed.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
If, for some \(k\),
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:future-rank}
 \dim\operatorname{Span}\bigl(S_{\geq k}\cup R_{\geq k}(S)\bigr)
 <w_k,
\end{equation}
then \(S\) cannot be extended to a compatible basis.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For any completion \(\mathcal B\) of \(S\),
\[
 \mathcal B_{\geq k}
 \subseteq
 S_{\geq k}\cup R_{\geq k}(S).
\]
Hence
\[
 \dim\operatorname{Span}(\mathcal B_{\geq k})
 \leq
 \dim\operatorname{Span}\bigl(S_{\geq k}\cup R_{\geq k}(S)\bigr).
\]
If the latter dimension is smaller than
\(w_k=\dim W_k\), then
\(\operatorname{Span}(\mathcal B_{\geq k})\neq W_k\).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The future-rank condition is necessary but not sufficient for
extendability, since \(R_{\geq k}(S)\) may contain several candidates
from the same unassigned representative family. Thus
\[
 \dim\operatorname{Span}\bigl(S_{\geq k}\cup R_{\geq k}(S)\bigr)
\]
is only an upper bound on the tail rank attainable by a completion.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:correctness}
The baseline algorithm and the modified algorithm return a compatible
basis if and only if such a basis exists.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Suppose first that either algorithm returns a complete selection.
Exactly one vector has then been chosen from each representative
family, and the independence test guarantees that the resulting
\(d\) vectors form a basis.

For every block \(B_j\), the search enforces the upper bound \(r_j\).
Since
\[
 \sum_{j=k_0}^{n} r_j=d,
\]
a complete selection of \(d\) vectors satisfying these bounds must
use exactly \(r_j\) vectors from each block \(B_j\). By
Proposition~\ref{prop:quota-characterization}, the resulting basis is
therefore compatible with the tail-space flag.

Conversely, suppose that a compatible basis \(\mathcal B\) exists.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:trimming}, it uses only the blocks
\(B_{k_0},\ldots,B_n\), so all of its vectors occur in the candidate
lists considered by the search. Hence \(\mathcal B\) determines a
branch of the search tree.

No partial selection along this branch is rejected by the independence
test, since every subfamily of a basis is linearly independent.
Moreover, Proposition~\ref{prop:required} shows that the branch never
exceeds any block quota.

It remains to consider the additional future-rank test used by the
modified algorithm. Let \(S\) be a partial selection lying on the
branch determined by \(\mathcal B\). For any \(k\), every vector of
\(\mathcal B_{\geq k}\) is either already contained in
\(S_{\geq k}\) or belongs to an unassigned representative family in a
block whose quota has not yet been filled. Hence it is contained in
\(R_{\geq k}(S)\). Therefore
\[
 \mathcal B_{\geq k}
 \subseteq
 S_{\geq k}\cup R_{\geq k}(S).
\]
Since \(\mathcal B\) is compatible,
\(\operatorname{Span}(\mathcal B_{\geq k})=W_k\), and consequently
\[
 \dim\operatorname{Span}\bigl(S_{\geq k}\cup R_{\geq k}(S)\bigr)
 \geq w_k.
\]
Thus the future-rank test never rejects this branch.

The branch corresponding to \(\mathcal B\) therefore remains in the
finite search tree and is eventually reached by both algorithms.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
For
\(B=\big[\, A^{N-1}G\mid A^{N-2}G\mid\cdots\mid G\,\big]\), the modified algorithm
returns a solution if and only if there exists a
reachability-profile preserving single-use actuator schedule.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:exponential-separation}
For \(m\geq1\), let
\[
 A_m=I_m\otimes A_0,
 \qquad
 \widetilde G_m=I_m\otimes G_0,
\]
and obtain \(G_m\) from \(\widetilde G_m\) by the column permutation
\[
 \pi_m=
 (1,4,\ldots,3m-2,\;
  2,5,\ldots,3m-1,\;
  3,6,\ldots,3m).
\]
Thus the actuators are ordered by type: first all type--\(1\)
actuators, then all type--\(2\), and finally all type--\(3\).

For horizon \(N=3\), set \(B_j=A_m^{3-j}G_m\). Then
\[
 (w_1,w_2,w_3)=(3m,3m,2m),
 \qquad
 (r_1,r_2,r_3)=(0,m,2m).
\]
With the ordering above, the baseline search visits
\[
 N_{\mathrm{base}}(m)=3\cdot2^m+m-2
\]
nodes before finding its first compatible basis, whereas the search
with future-rank pruning visits
\[
 N_{\mathrm{future}}(m)=3m+1.
\]
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Write
\[
 V=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m,
 \qquad
 V_r=\operatorname{Span}\{e_{r,1},e_{r,2},e_{r,3}\}.
\]
In the \(r\)-th summand, the three actuator vectors and their images
under \(A_m\) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 g_{r,1}&=e_{r,1},
 & A_mg_{r,1}&=-e_{r,3},\\
 g_{r,2}&=e_{r,2},
 & A_mg_{r,2}&=e_{r,1}+e_{r,3},\\
 g_{r,3}&=e_{r,1}+e_{r,2},
 & A_mg_{r,3}&=e_{r,1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The vectors in block \(3\) span
\(\operatorname{Span}\{e_{r,1},e_{r,2}\}\) in each summand, so \(w_3=2m\).
Adding block \(2\) supplies the missing direction \(e_{r,3}\), hence
\(W_2=V\) and \(w_2=3m\). Also \(w_1=3m\). Therefore
\[
 (w_1,w_2,w_3)=(3m,3m,2m),
 \qquad
 (r_1,r_2,r_3)=(0,m,2m),
\]
and \(k_0=2\).

We first consider the baseline search. Because the actuators are
ordered by type, the first \(m\) representative families are of
type~\(1\). Their first candidates are the block--\(3\) vectors
\(e_{r,1}\), which are mutually independent and belong to the branch
leading to the first solution. Hence exactly one node is visited at
each depth \(0,\ldots,m\).

For a type--\(2\) actuator, the two candidates in the trimmed problem
are
\[
 e_{r,2}\quad\text{from block }3,
 \qquad
 e_{r,1}+e_{r,3}\quad\text{from block }2.
\]
Both are independent of the previously selected \(e_{r,1}\), and at
this stage neither choice violates a block quota. Thus each
type--\(2\) actuator doubles the number of surviving branches. After
\(s\) such actuators, there are \(2^s\) nodes at depth \(m+s\), so
\[
 N_k=2^{k-m},
 \qquad m<k\leq2m.
\]

For a type--\(3\) actuator, the candidates are
\[
 e_{r,1}+e_{r,2}\quad\text{from block }3,
 \qquad
 e_{r,1}\quad\text{from block }2.
\]
The block--\(2\) candidate is always dependent on the previously
selected type--\(1\) vector \(e_{r,1}\). The block--\(3\) candidate
is admissible exactly when the corresponding type--\(2\) actuator was
chosen from block \(2\). Indeed,
\[
 \{e_{r,1},e_{r,2},e_{r,1}+e_{r,2}\}
\]
is dependent, whereas
\[
 \{e_{r,1},e_{r,1}+e_{r,3},e_{r,1}+e_{r,2}\}
\]
is independent.

Each processed type--\(3\) actuator therefore eliminates one half of
the remaining branches. Hence
\[
 N_k=2^{3m-k},
 \qquad 2m<k\leq3m.
\]
The complete depth profile is
\[
 N_k=
 \begin{cases}
 1, & 0\leq k\leq m,\\
 2^{k-m}, & m<k\leq2m,\\
 2^{3m-k}, & 2m<k\leq3m.
 \end{cases}
\]
Summing over the depths gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 N_{\mathrm{base}}(m)
 &=(m+1)
   +\sum_{s=1}^{m}2^s
   +\sum_{s=1}^{m}2^{m-s} \\
 &=3\cdot2^m+m-2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now consider future-rank pruning. Suppose that a type--\(2\) actuator
in \(V_r\) is tentatively chosen from block \(3\). The selected
directions in this summand are then \(e_{r,1}\) and \(e_{r,2}\).
The only remaining actuator is of type~\(3\), whose possible vectors
are \(e_{r,1}\) and \(e_{r,1}+e_{r,2}\). Thus every direction still
available in \(V_r\) lies in
\(\operatorname{Span}\{e_{r,1},e_{r,2}\}\), so the attainable contribution of this
summand to the level--\(2\) rank is at most \(2\).

The remaining \(m-1\) summands contribute at most \(3(m-1)\)
dimensions. Therefore the total attainable rank is at most
\[
 2+3(m-1)=3m-1<w_2=3m.
\]
The future-rank test rejects the block--\(3\) choice immediately.

Consequently, every type--\(2\) actuator is forced into block \(2\).
After these choices, the type--\(3\) block--\(3\) candidates are
independent of the previously selected vectors. The search therefore
follows a single recursive branch through depths \(0,\ldots,3m\), and
hence
\[
 N_{\mathrm{future}}(m)=3m+1.
\]
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
A visited node means a call to the recursive DFS procedure. A
candidate rejected by a quota, independence, or future-rank test does
not create a new visited node.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The formulas in Proposition~\ref{prop:exponential-separation} refer to
the fixed actuator and candidate ordering above and to the search for
the first solution. They are not order-independent worst-case bounds.
They exhibit a structured family for which future-rank pruning changes
the first-solution search tree from exponential to linear size.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
